Exposition

Hyperbolic Gaussians: shells, the effective radius, and two critical scales

Source paper
This explanation is based on the public version arXiv:2607.27605v1

This page is an explanation, not the original paper.

An exposition of my paper Radial Hyperbolic Measures: Shell Geometry, Pyramid Limits, and Gaussian Phase Transitions, arXiv:2607.27605v1. The subject is the pyramid limit (Theorem 1.1) of a rotationally symmetric probability measure in high-dimensional hyperbolic space when distances are shrunk, and its application to two kinds of hyperbolic Gaussian, which yields the two critical scalings n−1n^{-1}n−1 and n−1/2n^{-1/2}n−1/2 (Table 1, Corollaries 5.3 and 6.3). Numbering of definitions, theorems and equations follows this public version dated 30 July 2026. In running text the paper sometimes calls propositions, corollaries and lemmas "Theorem"; this page uses the label that matches the kind of statement.

The prerequisites are calculus, linear algebra, metric spaces and basic probability. I introduce mm-spaces and pyramids only as far as each step needs them. Long computations and proof details sit in collapsible blocks. The background theorems (Shioya's [5] book, Nakajima [3], Ozawa–Shioya [4], and Yokota's earlier paper) are used as inputs, as in the paper, and are not proved here. This page is not an independent complete proof.

Boxed theorems and lemmas are the paper's statements. Paragraphs beginning "Explainer's note.", as well as worked examples and numerical substitutions, are additions for readability and are not statements of the paper. Where the paper's text was incomplete and I filled the gap, the note begins "Distinction from the source."

Question | Two Gaussians with the same name have different critical scalings of distance

In Euclidean Rn\mathbb R^nRn, choosing points with density e−∣x∣2/(2σ2)e^{-|x|^2/(2\sigma^2)}e−∣x∣2/(2σ2) and placing independent normal coordinates of mean 000 and variance σ2\sigma^2σ2 give the same distribution. In hyperbolic space Hn\mathbb H^nHn of curvature −1-1−1, these two constructions give different distributions. The one built as a density with respect to volume is the Riemannian Gaussian; the one obtained by wrapping a Gaussian on the tangent space is the wrapped Gaussian.

Let the dimension nnn grow and multiply distances by a positive number αn\alpha_nαn​. The limit then breaks down in one of two ways. If αn\alpha_nαn​ is small, every real-valued 111-Lipschitz observation becomes almost constant (concentration, the Lévy property). If αn\alpha_nαn​ is large, sets of positive probability can be pushed arbitrarily far apart (infinite dissipation). The scaling tnt_ntn​ at the boundary is the critical scaling. The question is: for the two Gaussians, what are the critical scalings, and what survives in the limit there?

The answer is as follows. The critical scaling is n−1n^{-1}n−1 for the Riemannian Gaussian and n−1/2n^{-1/2}n−1/2 for the wrapped Gaussian. At a constant multiple αn∼ctn\alpha_n\sim ct_nαn​∼ctn​ of the critical scaling, what remains is the family of all mm-spaces of diameter at most 2cσ22c\sigma^22cσ2 (Riemannian) or at most 2cσ2c\sigma2cσ (wrapped) (Table 1). That the radii of the points concentrate in different places is easy to accept, but to read the size of the limit from the radius one needs the effective radius, which is the radius corrected by the loss due to angular concentration. This correction is the centre of the page.

The plan is as follows. First I fix the two Gaussians and rotationally symmetric measures, and prepare pyramids as the tool for comparing a sequence of spaces. Next I look at an example where concentration of the radius alone does not determine the limit, and then introduce the effective radius. After that I prove Theorem 1.1, apply it to the Gaussians, study the behaviour above and below the critical scalings, and finally relate the effective radius to curvature.

Tool | Spaces of different dimension are compared through their families of observations, the pyramids

The sequence Xn=(Hn,…)X_n=(\mathbb H^n,\ldots)Xn​=(Hn,…) consists of different spaces for different nnn, so one cannot superpose points to take a "limit of spaces". Instead of the spaces themselves, I compare the totality of observations that can be extracted from them. This section prepares that tool.

A pair of a metric space and a Borel probability measure on it is called an mm-space, written X=(X,dX,μX)X=(X,d_X,\mu_X)X=(X,dX​,μX​). The metric space is complete and separable, and the measure has full support.

Distinction from the source. The introduction of v1 defines an mm-space as a complete separable metric space with a Borel probability measure, and does not state a support condition. On the other hand XnX_nXn​ is taken on supp⁡μn\operatorname{supp}\mu_nsuppμn​, and the proof of Theorem 3.4 uses that "μY\mu_YμY​ has full support". I read the full-support condition as part of the definition.

For s>0s>0s>0, sXsXsX denotes the space with distances multiplied by sss and the measure unchanged. A map f:X→Yf:X\to Yf:X→Y is 111-Lipschitz if dY(f(x),f(x′))≤dX(x,x′)d_Y(f(x),f(x'))\leq d_X(x,x')dY​(f(x),f(x′))≤dX​(x,x′) for all points. If there is a 111-Lipschitz map with f∗μX=μYf_*\mu_X=\mu_Yf∗​μX​=μY​, we say that XXX dominates YYY and write Y≺XY\prec XY≺X. The push-forward is defined by f∗μX(B)=μX(f−1(B))f_*\mu_X(B)=\mu_X(f^{-1}(B))f∗​μX​(B)=μX​(f−1(B)).

The family of all mm-spaces dominated by XXX is the pyramid P(X)\mathcal P(X)P(X) of XXX; it records every way of measuring XXX. The families that will appear as limits are, for D≥0D\geq0D≥0,

P≤D={Y∣Y is an mm-space with diam⁡Y≤D}. \mathcal P_{\leq D} =\{Y\mid Y\text{ is an mm-space with }\operatorname{diam}Y\leq D\}. P≤D​={Y∣Y is an mm-space with diamY≤D}.

Here diam⁡Y=sup⁡y,y′∈YdY(y,y′)\operatorname{diam}Y=\sup_{y,y'\in Y}d_Y(y,y')diamY=supy,y′∈Y​dY​(y,y′) is the diameter. The family P≤D\mathcal P_{\leq D}P≤D​ is not attached to a particular space; it prescribes only an upper bound on the diameter. For D=0D=0D=0 it consists of one-point spaces only. For a pyramid Q\mathcal QQ and c>0c>0c>0, put cQ={cY∣Y∈Q}c\mathcal Q=\{cY\mid Y\in\mathcal Q\}cQ={cY∣Y∈Q}. In particular cP≤D=P≤cDc\mathcal P_{\leq D}=\mathcal P_{\leq cD}cP≤D​=P≤cD​.

To define convergence of a sequence of pyramids we need a notion of closeness of mm-spaces. For two spaces X,YX,YX,Y, a coupling is a probability measure π\piπ on X×YX\times YX×Y whose marginals are μX\mu_XμX​ and μY\mu_YμY​. For a closed set S⊂X×YS\subset X\times YS⊂X×Y its distortion is

dis⁡S=sup⁡(x,y),(x′,y′)∈S∣dX(x,x′)−dY(y,y′)∣, \operatorname{dis}S =\sup_{(x,y),(x',y')\in S}|d_X(x,x')-d_Y(y,y')|, disS=(x,y),(x′,y′)∈Ssup​∣dX​(x,x′)−dY​(y,y′)∣,

□(X,Y)=inf⁡π,Smax⁡{1−π(S),dis⁡S} \Box(X,Y)=\inf_{\pi,S}\max\{1-\pi(S),\operatorname{dis}S\} □(X,Y)=π,Sinf​max{1−π(S),disS}

(Nakajima's [3] characterization by couplings). If there are a coupling and a closed set with π(S)≥1−δ\pi(S)\geq1-\deltaπ(S)≥1−δ and dis⁡S≤η\operatorname{dis}S\leq\etadisS≤η, then □(X,Y)≤max⁡{δ,η}\Box(X,Y)\leq\max\{\delta,\eta\}□(X,Y)≤max{δ,η}. In words: apart from an exceptional set of small probability, corresponding pairs of points have almost equal distances.

A sequence of pyramids Pn\mathcal P_nPn​ converges weakly to Q\mathcal QQ if, in the box distance, (i) every space of Q\mathcal QQ is a limit of a sequence of spaces from Pn\mathcal P_nPn​, and (ii) whenever a subsequence from Pnk\mathcal P_{n_k}Pnk​​ converges, its limit lies in Q\mathcal QQ (Painlevé–Kuratowski convergence). I use two background facts, which the paper cites.

  • (B1) Suppose □(Xn,Yn)→0\Box(X_n,Y_n)\to0□(Xn​,Yn​)→0. If the pyramids P(Yn)\mathcal P(Y_n)P(Yn​) converge weakly to Q\mathcal QQ, then so do P(Xn)\mathcal P(X_n)P(Xn​), to the same Q\mathcal QQ (Shioya [5], Proposition 5.5 and Theorem 6.25).
  • (B2) The weak topology on the set of all pyramids is compact and metrizable (Shioya [5], Theorem 6.22). Hence if all subsequential limits coincide, the whole sequence converges.

Explainer's note. By (B1), replacing a measure by another one does not change the pyramid limit as long as the box distance tends to 000. This replacement is used in Step 1 of the proof of Theorem 1.1.

Obstacle | Even if the radius concentrates at one value, the pyramid limit cannot be read off the raw radius

The tool is ready, so consider a radial measure whose radius concentrates. If Rn\mathbf R_nRn​ gathers around a fixed value, then after multiplying distances by sns_nsn​ the points lie almost on a shell of radius snρns_n\rho_nsn​ρn​, and the limit pyramid looks like P≤2snρn\mathcal P_{\leq2s_n\rho_n}P≤2sn​ρn​​. Yet the introduction of the paper gives an example where this fails.

Let μn\mu_nμn​ be the uniform probability measure on the geodesic sphere of radius ρn=log⁡n\rho_n=\log nρn​=logn, and let sn=1/log⁡ns_n=1/\log nsn​=1/logn. The radial width is 000 from the start, and the scaled radius is snρn=1s_n\rho_n=1sn​ρn​=1. The raw radius suggests that the family of diameter at most 222 survives. But the paper asserts

P(snXn)⟶P≤1, \mathcal P(s_nX_n)\longrightarrow\mathcal P_{\leq1}, P(sn​Xn​)⟶P≤1​,

and moreover that the distances among any fixed number of independently chosen points all converge to 222 in probability. This follows from Theorem 1.1 and Proposition 3.3 (introduction). The limit is the family of diameter at most 111, while sample distances are 222; the two seem to disagree.

Explainer's note. The two disagree because "pairs of points" and "sets of positive probability" see different things. The inner product of two independent directions is of order 1/n1/\sqrt n1/n​, so they are almost orthogonal, and a sample pair is almost surely as far apart as "passing through the centre" allows. The pyramid, on the other hand, records how far sets of positive probability can be pulled apart. As the lemma below shows, for two sets of fixed mass on the sphere there is always a pair of points whose distance, measured in the chord length multiplied by n\sqrt nn​, is bounded by a constant. For such a close pair, the two points branch off from the direction of the centre at a radius of about 12log⁡n\tfrac12\log n21​logn, so the round trip is shorter by log⁡n\log nlogn. After multiplying by sn=1/log⁡ns_n=1/\log nsn​=1/logn, this difference is the difference between 222 and 111.

So the quantity that fixes the size of the limit is not the raw scaled radius snρns_n\rho_nsn​ρn​ but a quantity from which the 12log⁡n\tfrac12\log n21​logn due to angular concentration has been subtracted. The next section defines it and states the theorem.

Why is an,ρa_{n,\rho}an,ρ​ the right quantity? The next section proves Theorem 1.1 in four steps.

Proof | Replace the radius by a shell, then separate sets of positive probability on the shell

The proof of Theorem 1.1 proceeds as follows: (1) replace the measure by a single shell, (2) write the distance of the shell as a transform of the distance of the sphere, (3) measure the separation of sets of positive probability there to obtain the limit for deterministic shells, and (4) finish for general scalings and for the signed distance.

Step 1 | If the radial width vanishes, the measure may be replaced by a shell

Since (1.2) is assumed, I check that the measure itself can be replaced by a shell of radius ρn\rho_nρn​. The uniform shell of radius ρ>0\rho>0ρ>0 is

Σn,ρ=(Sn−1, dn,ρ, σn−1),dn,ρ(θ,η)=dH(tanh⁡(ρ/2)θ, tanh⁡(ρ/2)η) \Sigma_{n,\rho}=(S^{n-1},\ d_{n,\rho},\ \sigma_{n-1}),\qquad d_{n,\rho}(\theta,\eta)=d_{\mathbb H}\bigl(\tanh(\rho/2)\theta,\ \tanh(\rho/2)\eta\bigr) Σn,ρ​=(Sn−1, dn,ρ​, σn−1​),dn,ρ​(θ,η)=dH​(tanh(ρ/2)θ, tanh(ρ/2)η)

(equation (3.1)). The distance is that between two points in the ambient hyperbolic space, not along a path inside the sphere.

Proposition 3.1 (Radial coupling). For all sn>0s_n>0sn​>0, ρn>0\rho_n>0ρn​>0 and ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0,

□(snXn, snΣn,ρn)≤max⁡{2ε, P(sn∣Rn−ρn∣>ε)}. \Box(s_nX_n,\ s_n\Sigma_{n,\rho_n}) \leq\max\Bigl\{2\varepsilon,\ \mathbb P\bigl(s_n|\mathbf R_n-\rho_n|>\varepsilon\bigr)\Bigr\}. □(sn​Xn​, sn​Σn,ρn​​)≤max{2ε, P(sn​∣Rn​−ρn​∣>ε)}.

Distinction from the source. Steps 3 and 4 above rearrange, into a more readable order, the places the paper cites in its proofs of Theorems 3.4 and 1.1. In the paper (3.10) is a separate formula derived from combining cited results; this page uses only its conclusion as an input.

Theorem 1.1 applies to any radial measure whose radius concentrates. The next section applies it to the two Gaussians.

What happens if the scaling is moved away from these critical values? The next section treats the two cases, concentration and dissipation.

Consequence | Below the critical scaling the spaces concentrate; above it they dissipate

The Application section showed that at scalings n−1n^{-1}n−1 and n−1/2n^{-1/2}n−1/2 pyramids of finite diameter remain. It has not yet shown that smaller scalings give concentration and larger ones dissipation. In this section I define concentration and dissipation and state a criterion that derives the behaviour on both sides from the critical limit.

Interpretation | The rate at which the curvature of a shell decays gives the effective radius

So far the effective radius an,ρ=snlog⁡(sinh⁡ρ/n)a_{n,\rho}=s_n\log(\sinh\rho/\sqrt n)an,ρ​=sn​log(sinhρ/n​) has been a quantity defined from distances. Section 4 of the paper shows that the same quantity can also be read as the decay rate of the curvature of the shell. This section is another view of Theorem 1.1 and is not part of the main line of the proof.

The metric that determines lengths along the shell of radius ρ\rhoρ is sinh⁡2ρ\sinh^2\rhosinh2ρ times the metric of the unit sphere (equation (3.5)). Its intrinsic sectional curvature is therefore

Kn,ρΣ=1sinh⁡2ρ(n≥3). K^\Sigma_{n,\rho}=\frac1{\sinh^2\rho}\qquad(n\geq3). Kn,ρΣ​=sinh2ρ1​(n≥3).

Since An,ρ−2=nKn,ρΣA_{n,\rho}^{-2}=nK^\Sigma_{n,\rho}An,ρ−2​=nKn,ρΣ​ (equation (3.6)), the effective radius satisfies the identity

an,ρ=−sn2log⁡(nKn,ρΣ). a_{n,\rho}=-\frac{s_n}{2}\log\bigl(nK^\Sigma_{n,\rho}\bigr). an,ρ​=−2sn​​log(nKn,ρΣ​).

To check, note that −12log⁡(n/sinh⁡2ρ)=log⁡(sinh⁡ρ/n)-\tfrac12\log(n/\sinh^2\rho)=\log(\sinh\rho/\sqrt n)−21​log(n/sinh2ρ)=log(sinhρ/n​). The smaller the curvature, the larger the effective radius.

Distinction from the source. The paper states the sectional curvature in (3.5) without restricting nnn, but the sectional curvature of the sphere Sn−1S^{n-1}Sn−1 is defined only for n≥3n\geq3n≥3. I state n≥3n\geq3n≥3 explicitly. Since we take n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞, the conclusions are unaffected.

Limits | Even on the shell where tangential curvature vanishes, the ambient curvature stays −1-1−1

The previous section found a shell on which the weighted curvature vanishes. That phrasing is easily read as saying that the ambient curvature becomes flat. Remark 6.4 of the paper says that it cannot be read this way.

Remark 6.4 (What becomes flat and what vanishes exactly). The sectional curvature of the ambient hyperbolic space remains −1-1−1. The intrinsic sectional curvature of a modal shell is positive, and the tangential Bakry–Émery Ricci eigenvalue is (n−1)(n-1)(n−1) times it. On an exact zero-curvature shell, the radial weighted-Ricci eigenvalue equals the full trace, and its limit after division by nnn is −1-1−1. Hence even if the tangential part vanishes exactly, neither the ambient curvature nor the full weighted Ricci tensor vanishes.

Explainer's note. For the Riemannian type V′′=1/σ2V''=1/\sigma^2V′′=1/σ2 is constant and (V′′−(n−1))/n→−1(V''-(n-1))/n\to-1(V′′−(n−1))/n→−1, so this −1-1−1 can be checked directly. The shell of zero curvature does not mark a place where the whole geometry is flat; it marks the place where concentration occurs and only the tangential part vanishes.

The scope of this section and other limits are the following.

  • That the shell of vanishing tangential curvature is exponentially close to the modal shell is a feature of the Gaussian potential, not a property of radial densities in general (Remark 4.4). Convergence itself only requires that the sequence of radii lie within the same tolerance of the modal radius; curvature plays no role.
  • Theorem 4.2 assumes a finite limit a∈Ra\in\mathbb Ra∈R of the effective radius. The case a=−∞a=-\inftya=−∞ (collapse to a point) is covered by Theorem 1.1 alone.
  • Table 1 classifies the case where αn/tn\alpha_n/t_nαn​/tn​ converges to 000, to a finite positive value, or to ∞\infty∞. For sequences that do not converge, I assign no classification from the table.
  • I have not proved the background theorems (propositions and theorems of Shioya's [5] book, the coupling characterization of the box distance, the limit formula for observable diameter). They are used in the form cited by the paper.

The only mathematical source is the fixed public version Radial Hyperbolic Measures: Shell Geometry, Pyramid Limits, and Gaussian Phase Transitions, arXiv:2607.27605v1 dated 30 July 2026. The correspondence with this page is as follows.

The background literature cited in this table is limited to what the paper cites directly. The coupling characterization of the box distance is due to Nakajima; the general theory of mm-spaces, weak convergence of pyramids, concentration on the sphere and the lemmas on separation distance are from Shioya's book; the limit formula for observable diameter is Yokota (Geom. Dedicata 220, Theorem 1.1); and the homogeneity of separation distance is from Ozawa–Shioya.

The places marked "Distinction from the source" are three: (i) the reading of the support condition of mm-spaces, (ii) the arrangement of the steps in the proof of Theorem 1.1 and the treatment of (3.10), and (iii) the explicit n≥3n\geq3n≥3 for the sectional curvature of the shell. Where the paper's running text calls propositions, corollaries and lemmas "Theorem" (for example, referring to Proposition 3.1 as "Theorem 3.1"), this page uses the label of the kind of statement. Worked examples, numerical substitutions and explainer's notes serve this page's exposition; they are neither independent verification nor claims absent from the paper.
